cards.fix_question: State two rules for writing the binomial name of a species.
cards.fix_answer: The genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a lower-case letter. The name is in italics when printed or each word underlined when handwritten.

cards.reason: Sound fact; opener is not an exam word.
cards.fix_question: State why scientists use the binomial system.
cards.fix_answer: The binomial name of a species is the same in every country, so it identifies the species without the confusion caused by local common names.

cards.fix_question: State what is meant by a taxon.
cards.fix_answer: A taxon is a group of organisms placed together at one rank of a classification, for example a genus, a family or a class.

cards.fix_question: State the basis on which organisms are grouped in a natural classification.
cards.fix_answer: Homologous features and evolutionary relationships: the more homologous features organisms share, the more recently they shared a common ancestor and the more closely they are grouped.

cards.fix_question: Explain one limitation of the morphological species concept, using an example.
cards.fix_answer: Species can look almost identical yet be separate species. For example, some Drosophila species are very hard to tell apart by appearance but are kept separate by different courtship behaviour, so appearance alone cannot separate them.

cards.fix_question: Compare the maximum resolution and the maximum useful magnification of a light microscope with those of a transmission electron microscope.
cards.fix_answer: Light microscope: resolution about 200 nm (0.2 um), magnification up to about x1500. TEM: resolution of the order of 0.1 to 1 nm, magnification of several hundred thousand times or more. Both values are approximate.

cards.fix_question: State the equation for linear magnification and state what each symbol stands for.
cards.fix_answer: M = I / A, where M is magnification (no unit), I is the image size and A is the actual size, both in the same unit.

cards.fix_question: State how many micrometres are in 1 millimetre and how many nanometres are in 1 micrometre.
cards.fix_answer: 1 mm = 1000 um and 1 um = 1000 nm.

cards.fix_question: Explain why a light microscope cannot be used to see the cristae of a mitochondrion.
cards.fix_answer: The cristae are closer together than the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 200 nm), so they cannot be seen as separate structures; an electron microscope has the resolution needed.

Says ribosomes pass through nuclear pores; it is ribosomal subunits (a whole 80S ribosome is not assembled in the nucleus).
cards.fix_question: Describe the function of the nuclear envelope.
cards.fix_answer: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane that separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm. Nuclear pores control the movement of molecules such as mRNA and ribosomal subunits into and out of the nucleus.
cards.conflict: Ours 2.2-002 sends mRNA through the pore only; existing wording about whole ribosomes is wrong, subunits cross the pores.

cards.reason: What is the function opener; content accurate.
cards.fix_question: State the function of the nucleolus.
cards.fix_answer: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles it with proteins into ribosomal subunits.

cards.reason: Accurate: 80S in the cytoplasm and on RER (syllabus).

cards.fix_question: Compare the ribosomes in the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell with those in its mitochondria.
cards.fix_answer: Cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S and larger; mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S and smaller, and they lie in the mitochondrial matrix.

cards.reason: Opens with List; ribosome and RER listed as two steps.
cards.fix_question: Outline the route taken by a protein from its synthesis to its secretion from a eukaryotic cell.
cards.fix_answer: Made by ribosomes on the rough ER (from mRNA copied in the nucleus), enters the RER, passes in transport vesicles to the Golgi body, is modified and packaged into secretory vesicles, which fuse with the cell surface membrane and release it.
cards.conflict: Ours 2.2-025 supports the order RER, Golgi, membrane; agree.

cards.fix_question: Suggest two organelles that would be abundant in a pancreatic cell that secretes large amounts of digestive enzymes, and explain each choice.
cards.fix_answer: Rough ER, to make large amounts of protein on its many ribosomes; Golgi body, to modify and package the enzymes into secretory vesicles.

cards.fix_question: State the function of the tonoplast.
cards.fix_answer: The tonoplast is the membrane around the large permanent vacuole; it is partially permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the vacuole.

cards.fix_question: State five molecular components of the cell surface membrane.
cards.fix_answer: Phospholipids, cholesterol, glycolipids, proteins (channel and carrier proteins) and glycoproteins.

cards.reason: Says the bilayer is impermeable to most ions and polar molecules; that is an unqualified universal.
cards.fix_question: Describe the role of phospholipids in the cell surface membrane.
cards.fix_answer: Phospholipids form a bilayer with hydrophilic heads facing the water on both sides and hydrophobic tails facing inwards. The hydrophobic core is a barrier to the passage of most ions and polar molecules.

cards.reason: Mechanism at low temperature is wrong (restricting movement does not stop rigidity).
cards.fix_question: Describe the role of cholesterol in the cell surface membrane.
cards.fix_answer: Cholesterol fits between phospholipids and regulates membrane fluidity: at higher temperature it restricts phospholipid movement and at lower temperature it stops the phospholipids packing closely together.

cards.reason: Asks for two differences but gives a table of three; speed row is not a syllabus point.
cards.fix_question: State two differences between channel proteins and carrier proteins.
cards.fix_answer: A channel protein forms a fixed water-filled pore, whereas a carrier protein binds a specific molecule and changes shape. Channel proteins are used only in facilitated diffusion, whereas carrier proteins are used in facilitated diffusion and active transport.

cards.fix_question: Suggest what would happen if a drug that binds to a cell surface receptor without activating it were given with the normal signalling molecule.
cards.fix_answer: The drug acts as an antagonist: it occupies the receptor binding site, so the normal signalling molecule cannot bind and the response is reduced or blocked.
